bug_report.Title: BlockMatrix multiplication turns ZeroMatrix blocks into scalar Zero causing AttributeError
bug_report.Description: Multiplying a BlockMatrix that contains ZeroMatrix blocks can produce scalar S.Zero entries where matrix-typed blocks are expected; subsequent BlockMatrix operations access .rows/.cols on those scalar entries and raise AttributeError ('Zero' object has no attribute 'cols').
bug_report.RootCause:
1) BlockMatrix._blockmul (sympy/matrices/expressions/blockmatrix.py) constructs and returns BlockMatrix(self.blocks * other.blocks) directly when block sizes align (code: "return BlockMatrix(self.blocks*other.blocks)"). This assumes that block-wise multiplication of the underlying block storage yields matrix-typed block entries, but the underlying matrix-entry construction and simplification can produce scalar S.Zero instead of a ZeroMatrix object.

2) BlockMatrix._blockadd (sympy/matrices/expressions/blockmatrix.py) analogously constructs and returns BlockMatrix(self.blocks + other.blocks) without ensuring entries remain matrix-typed (code: "return BlockMatrix(self.blocks + other.blocks)"). Sums of ZeroMatrix entries can collapse to scalar S.Zero during canonicalization.

3) DenseMatrix._eval_matrix_mul (sympy/matrices/dense.py) constructs each dense matrix multiplication entry as Add(*products) (code: "new_mat[i] = Add(*vec)"). Because entries are built via Add, matrix-add canonicalization can later simplify those Adds.

4) MatAdd canonicalization (sympy/matrices/expressions/matadd.py) includes an identity-removal rule that treats both scalar zero and ZeroMatrix as identities (code: "rm_id(lambda x: x == 0 or isinstance(x, ZeroMatrix))"). This can remove ZeroMatrix summands from an Add, leaving Add() -> scalar S.Zero. That is the mechanism by which an entry that semantically represents a zero matrix becomes scalar S.Zero.

5) BlockMatrix.rowblocksizes and BlockMatrix.colblocksizes (sympy/matrices/expressions/blockmatrix.py) encode the invariant that every block is a Matrix-like object by accessing block.rows and block.cols directly (code: "return [self.blocks[i, 0].rows ...]" and "return [self.blocks[0, i].cols ...]"). When a block entry has been simplified to scalar S.Zero, these properties raise AttributeError because scalar Zero lacks .rows/.cols.

6) Callers that depend on the BlockMatrix invariant are part of the failing path: block_collapse -> bc_matmul/bc_matadd (sympy/matrices/expressions/blockmatrix.py, e.g. bc_matmul calls A._blockmul(B)) ultimately rely on BlockMatrix._blockmul/_blockadd to preserve matrix-typed blocks. The stack trace in the original report shows the failure occurring when colblocksizes attempted to access .cols on a scalar zero.

7) Related sibling implementations such as BlockDiagMatrix._blockmul/_blockadd (sympy/matrices/expressions/blockmatrix.py) are relevant to the scope: BlockDiagMatrix performs elementwise operations on diagonal blocks and falls back to BlockMatrix implementations for other cases; the same collapse-to-scalar-zero behavior in intermediate MatAdd/MatMul expressions can affect BlockDiagMatrix results and any other code paths that rely on the BlockMatrix invariant.

Diagnostic relationship (intended invariant, not a code patch): results of block-wise arithmetic that are intended to represent the zero matrix at some (i,j) block must be represented as a MatrixExpr zero (ZeroMatrix) of the appropriate block shape. Concretely, a scalar S.Zero present at BlockMatrix.blocks[i, j] indicates the block-size invariant has been violated: that scalar should be interpreted as ZeroMatrix(rowblocksizes[i], colblocksizes[j]) for arithmetic results that are block matrices.
StepsToReproduce: from sympy import MatrixSymbol, ZeroMatrix, BlockMatrix, block_collapse
block_collapse(b * b * b)  # raises AttributeError: 'Zero' object has no attribute 'cols'
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Repeated block multiplication and addition on a BlockMatrix containing ZeroMatrix blocks should succeed without raising AttributeError. Zero blocks should remain matrix-typed (i.e., represented as ZeroMatrix with the correct block shape) so that block_collapse(b * b * b) returns the expected matrix result (e.g. top-left a**2 and zeros elsewhere) rather than raising an exception.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Multiplying the BlockMatrix once (b * b) yields the expected result, but multiplying it again (b * b * b or block_collapse(b * b * b)) raises AttributeError: 'Zero' object has no attribute 'cols' because some block entries have been simplified to scalar S.Zero instead of ZeroMatrix objects.

"""Geometrical Points.

Contains
========
Point
Point2D
Point3D

When methods of Point require 1 or more points as arguments, they
can be passed as a sequence of coordinates or Points:

>>> from sympy.geometry.point import Point
>>> Point(1, 1).is_collinear((2, 2), (3, 4))
False
>>> Point(1, 1).is_collinear(Point(2, 2), Point(3, 4))
False

"""

from __future__ import division, print_function

import warnings

from sympy.core import S, sympify, Expr
from sympy.core.compatibility import is_sequence
from sympy.core.containers import Tuple
from sympy.simplify import nsimplify, simplify
from sympy.geometry.exceptions import GeometryError
from sympy.functions.elementary.miscellaneous import sqrt
from sympy.functions.elementary.complexes import im
from sympy.matrices import Matrix
from sympy.core.numbers import Float
from sympy.core.evaluate import global_evaluate
from sympy.core.add import Add
from sympy.utilities.iterables import uniq
from sympy.utilities.misc import filldedent, func_name, Undecidable

from .entity import GeometryEntity


class Point(GeometryEntity):
    """A point in a n-dimensional Euclidean space.

    Parameters
    ==========

    coords : sequence of n-coordinate values. In the special
        case where n=2 or 3, a Point2D or Point3D will be created
        as appropriate.
    evaluate : if `True` (default), all floats are turn into
        exact types.
    dim : number of coordinates the point should have.  If coordinates
        are unspecified, they are padded with zeros.
    on_morph : indicates what should happen when the number of
        coordinates of a point need to be changed by adding or
        removing zeros.  Possible values are `'warn'`, `'error'`, or
        `ignore` (default).  No warning or error is given when `*args`
        is empty and `dim` is given. An error is always raised when
        trying to remove nonzero coordinates.


    Attributes
    ==========

    length
    origin: A `Point` representing the origin of the
        appropriately-dimensioned space.

    Raises
    ======

    TypeError : When instantiating with anything but a Point or sequence
    ValueError : when instantiating with a sequence with length < 2 or
        when trying to reduce dimensions if keyword `on_morph='error'` is
        set.

    See Also
    ========

    sympy.geometry.line.Segment : Connects two Points

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy.geometry import Point
    >>> from sympy.abc import x
    >>> Point(1, 2, 3)
    Point3D(1, 2, 3)
    >>> Point([1, 2])
    Point2D(1, 2)
    >>> Point(0, x)
    Point2D(0, x)
    >>> Point(dim=4)
    Point(0, 0, 0, 0)

    Floats are automatically converted to Rational unless the
    evaluate flag is False:

    >>> Point(0.5, 0.25)
    Point2D(1/2, 1/4)
    >>> Point(0.5, 0.25, evaluate=False)
    Point2D(0.5, 0.25)

    """

    is_Point = True

    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        evaluate = kwargs.get('evaluate', global_evaluate[0])
        on_morph = kwargs.get('on_morph', 'ignore')

        # unpack into coords
        coords = args[0] if len(args) == 1 else args

        # check args and handle quickly handle Point instances
        if isinstance(coords, Point):
            # even if we're mutating the dimension of a point, we
            # don't reevaluate its coordinates
            evaluate = False
            if len(coords) == kwargs.get('dim', len(coords)):
                return coords

        if not is_sequence(coords):
            raise TypeError(filldedent('''
                Expecting sequence of coordinates, not `{}`'''
                                       .format(func_name(coords))))
        # A point where only `dim` is specified is initialized
        # to zeros.
        if len(coords) == 0 and kwargs.get('dim', None):
            coords = (S.Zero,)*kwargs.get('dim')

        coords = Tuple(*coords)
        dim = kwargs.get('dim', len(coords))

        if len(coords) < 2:
            raise ValueError(filldedent('''
                Point requires 2 or more coordinates or
                keyword `dim` > 1.'''))
        if len(coords) != dim:
            message = ("Dimension of {} needs to be changed "
                       "from {} to {}.").format(coords, len(coords), dim)
            if on_morph == 'ignore':
                pass
            elif on_morph == "error":
                raise ValueError(message)
            elif on_morph == 'warn':
                warnings.warn(message)
            else:
                raise ValueError(filldedent('''
                        on_morph value should be 'error',
                        'warn' or 'ignore'.'''))
        if any(coords[dim:]):
            raise ValueError('Nonzero coordinates cannot be removed.')
        if any(a.is_number and im(a) for a in coords):
            raise ValueError('Imaginary coordinates are not permitted.')
        if not all(isinstance(a, Expr) for a in coords):
            raise TypeError('Coordinates must be valid SymPy expressions.')

        # pad with zeros appropriately
        coords = coords[:dim] + (S.Zero,)*(dim - len(coords))

        # Turn any Floats into rationals and simplify
        # any expressions before we instantiate
        if evaluate:
            coords = coords.xreplace(dict(
                [(f, simplify(nsimplify(f, rational=True)))
                 for f in coords.atoms(Float)]))

        # return 2D or 3D instances
        if len(coords) == 2:
            kwargs['_nocheck'] = True
            return Point2D(*coords, **kwargs)
        elif len(coords) == 3:
            kwargs['_nocheck'] = True
            return Point3D(*coords, **kwargs)

        # the general Point
        return GeometryEntity.__new__(cls, *coords)

    def __abs__(self):
        """Returns the distance between this point and the origin."""
        origin = Point([0]*len(self))
        return Point.distance(origin, self)

    def __add__(self, other):
        """Add other to self by incrementing self's coordinates by
        those of other.

        Notes
        =====

        >>> from sympy.geometry.point import Point

        When sequences of coordinates are passed to Point methods, they
        are converted to a Point internally. This __add__ method does
        not do that so if floating point values are used, a floating
        point result (in terms of SymPy Floats) will be returned.

        >>> Point(1, 2) + (.1, .2)
        Point2D(1.1, 2.2)

        If this is not desired, the `translate` method can be used or
        another Point can be added:

        >>> Point(1, 2).translate(.1, .2)
        Point2D(11/10, 11/5)
        >>> Point(1, 2) + Point(.1, .2)
        Point2D(11/10, 11/5)

        See Also
        ========

        sympy.geometry.point.Point.translate

        """
        try:
            s, o = Point._normalize_dimension(self, Point(other, evaluate=False))
        except TypeError:
            raise GeometryError("Don't know how to add {} and a Point object".format(other))

        coords = [simplify(a + b) for a, b in zip(s, o)]
        return Point(coords, evaluate=False)

    def __contains__(self, item):
        return item in self.args

    def __div__(self, divisor):
        """Divide point's coordinates by a factor."""
        divisor = sympify(divisor)
        coords = [simplify(x/divisor) for x in self.args]
        return Point(coords, evaluate=False)

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Point) or len(self.args) != len(other.args):
            return False
        return self.args == other.args

    def __getitem__(self, key):
        return self.args[key]

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash(self.args)

    def __iter__(self):
        return self.args.__iter__()

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.args)

    def __mul__(self, factor):
        """Multiply point's coordinates by a factor.

        Notes
        =====

        >>> from sympy.geometry.point import Point

        When multiplying a Point by a floating point number,
        the coordinates of the Point will be changed to Floats:

        >>> Point(1, 2)*0.1
        Point2D(0.1, 0.2)

        If this is not desired, the `scale` method can be used or
        else only multiply or divide by integers:

        >>> Point(1, 2).scale(1.1, 1.1)
        Point2D(11/10, 11/5)
        >>> Point(1, 2)*11/10
        Point2D(11/10, 11/5)

        See Also
        ========

        sympy.geometry.point.Point.scale
        """
        factor = sympify(factor)
        coords = [simplify(x*factor) for x in self.args]
        return Point(coords, evaluate=False)

    def __neg__(self):
        """Negate the point."""
        coords = [-x for x in self.args]
        return Point(coords, evaluate=False)

    def __sub__(self, other):
        """Subtract two points, or subtract a factor from this point's
        coordinates."""
        return self + [-x for x in other]

    @classmethod
    def _normalize_dimension(cls, *points, **kwargs):
        """Ensure that points have the same dimension.
        By default `on_morph='warn'` is passed to the
        `Point` constructor."""
        # if we have a built-in ambient dimension, use it
        dim = getattr(cls, '_ambient_dimension', None)
        # override if we specified it
        dim = kwargs.get('dim', dim)
        # if no dim was given, use the highest dimensional point
        if dim is None:
            dim = max(i.ambient_dimension for i in points)
        if all(i.ambient_dimension == dim for i in points):
            return list(points)
        kwargs['dim'] = dim
        kwargs['on_morph'] = kwargs.get('on_morph', 'warn')
        return [Point(i, **kwargs) for i in points]

    @staticmethod
    def affine_rank(*args):
        """The affine rank of a set of points is the dimension
        of the smallest affine space containing all the points.
        For example, if the points lie on a line (and are not all
        the same) their affine rank is 1.  If the points lie on a plane
        but not a line, their affine rank is 2.  By convention, the empty
        set has affine rank -1."""

        if len(args) == 0:
            return -1
        # make sure we're genuinely points
        # and translate every point to the origin
        points = Point._normalize_dimension(*[Point(i) for i in args])
        origin = points[0]
        points = [i - origin for i in points[1:]]

        m = Matrix([i.args for i in points])
        # XXX fragile -- what is a better way?
        return m.rank(iszerofunc = lambda x:
            abs(x.n(2)) < 1e-12 if x.is_number else x.is_zero)

    @property
    def ambient_dimension(self):
        """Number of components this point has."""
        return getattr(self, '_ambient_dimension', len(self))

    @classmethod
    def are_coplanar(cls, *points):
        """Return True if there exists a plane in which all the points
        lie.  A trivial True value is returned if `len(points) < 3` or
        all Points are 2-dimensional.

        Parameters
        ==========

        A set of points

        Raises
        ======

        ValueError : if less than 3 unique points are given

        Returns
        =======

        boolean

        Examples
        ========

        >>> from sympy import Point3D
        >>> p1 = Point3D(1, 2, 2)
        >>> p2 = Point3D(2, 7, 2)
        >>> p3 = Point3D(0, 0, 2)
        >>> p4 = Point3D(1, 1, 2)
        >>> Point3D.are_coplanar(p1, p2, p3, p4)

bug_report.Title: GeometryError when adding Point and numeric*Point (order-dependent multiplication)
bug_report.Description: Adding a Point to a left-multiplied Point expression (e.g. point1 + 2.0*point2) raises an exception while the equivalent right-multiplied expression (point1 + point2*2.0) succeeds. The failure occurs because the Point constructor rejects non-sequence Expr inputs such as Mul(scalar, Point).
bug_report.RootCause:
1. sympy/geometry/entity.py:GeometryEntity.__rmul__ encodes the wrong dispatch assumption: it delegates reversed multiplication to the left operand by returning a.__mul__(self). Because Float.__mul__(Point) produces Mul(2.0, Point(...)), the result is a Mul, not a Point. (Current code: return a.__mul__(self)). The correct relationship for reversed multiplication in this geometry context is to invoke the geometry object's multiplication implementation: self.__mul__(a) so scalar * Point uses Point.__mul__.

2. sympy/geometry/point.py:Point.__add__ encodes the assumption that the right-hand side is already a Point or a coordinate sequence. It calls Point(other, evaluate=False) which raises TypeError "Expecting sequence of coordinates, not `Mul`" when other is Mul(2.0, Point2D(1, 1)), and this is wrapped into a GeometryError. Point.__add__ therefore fails if reversed multiplication produced a Mul instead of a Point.

3. sympy/core/numbers.py:Float.__mul__ behaviour (left-operand numeric multiplication) produces a generic Mul when the other operand is a non-number Basic. This numeric-side behavior is correct for numbers generally but is incompatible with GeometryEntity.__rmul__ delegating to the numeric left operand; Float.__mul__ is not specialized to return geometry.Point objects, so delegating to it yields the wrong type (Mul(2.0, Point(...))).

4. sympy/geometry/point.py:Point.__mul__ already implements the intended scalar*point semantics (it sympifies the factor and returns a Point with scaled coordinates). The existence of Point.__mul__ is evidence that reversed multiplication should call self.__mul__(a) rather than a.__mul__(self).
StepsToReproduce: python -c "from sympy import geometry as ge, sympify; p1 = ge.Point(0,0); p2 = ge.Point(1,1); print(p1 + p2 * sympify(2.0))"  # works
python -c "from sympy import geometry as ge, sympify; p1 = ge.Point(0,0); p2 = ge.Point(1,1); print(p1 + sympify(2.0) * p2)"  # raises GeometryError
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Both expressions (point1 + point2 * 2.0 and point1 + 2.0 * point2) should produce the same resulting Point and not raise an exception; scalar*Point and Point*scalar should be equivalent from the user's perspective.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: point1 + point2 * 2.0 returns a Point as expected. point1 + 2.0 * point2 raises GeometryError: "Don't know how to add 2.0*Point2D(1, 1) and a Point object" (originating from Point.__new__ raising TypeError: "Expecting sequence of coordinates, not `Mul`").

Checkpoint 5: Final report — root cause and complete fix

Root cause
- sympify (sympy/core/sympify.py) treats arbitrary non-string objects by calling unicode(a) and parse_expr on the result. parse_expr/eval_expr uses Python eval() to evaluate the expression text with SymPy's local/global environment. If an object has a repr that looks like a Python expression (e.g., "x" or "x.y"), sympify will evaluate that and may produce unintended results or invoke attribute access on existing objects (leading to exceptions or worse). Expr.__eq__ (sympy/core/expr.py) calls sympify(other) non-strictly during equality checks and thus can trigger this unsafe path when comparing a SymPy expression to an arbitrary object.

2. Documentation change (minor)

Why this change is complete (addresses every affected location)
- The misbehavior occurs because sympify unconditionally parsed unicode(a) for arbitrary objects. That is a single code path in sympify.py. Fixing it there prevents all callers (including Expr.__eq__) from indirectly evaluating object reprs.

This is safer and explicit.

Why no other files need to change
- parse_expr/eval_expr still do eval but only for strings passed explicitly. sympify's docstring warns about eval's dangers; our change makes the behavior consistent with that warning and removes the surprising/equivalence causing behavior for arbitrary objects.

bug_report.Title: SymPy evaluates arbitrary object's __repr__ during Expr.__eq__ (unsafe sympify fallback)
bug_report.Description: Equality comparisons of SymPy Expr objects can trigger parsing and evaluation of the repr() string of arbitrary Python objects. As a result, comparing a SymPy expression to an unrelated object can execute code derived from that object's __repr__, causing exceptions or incorrect equality results.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) sympy/core/sympify.py:sympify — incorrect assumption: sympify's "last chance" path treats any non-converted object by taking unicode(a) (the object's repr) and passing that string to the parser. Evidence: sympify imports compatibility.unicode and executes "a = unicode(a)" followed by a call to parse_expr(a, ...). Consequence: an object's repr like 'x.y' or 'x' becomes input to the parser/evaluator.

2) sympy/core/expr.py:Expr.__eq__ — incorrect assumption: Expr.__eq__ uses the non-strict sympify on arbitrary 'other' values and therefore can reach sympify's repr-parsing fallback. Evidence: Expr.__eq__ calls "other = sympify(other)" (no strict flag) inside a try/except that converts SympifyError/SyntaxError to False. Consequence: simple equality checks (e.g. Symbol('x') == C()) can cause the repr-to-code path to be exercised.

3) sympy/parsing/sympy_parser.py:eval_expr — incorrect assumption: code produced by the parser is safe to execute. Evidence: eval_expr executes the generated code with "expr = eval(code, global_dict, local_dict)", so strings that originated from an object's repr can be executed with SymPy globals/locals (e.g. "Symbol('x').y"). Consequence: attribute access or other runtime errors/side effects can occur as a direct result of an object's repr being parsed and evaluated.

4) sympy/core/basic.py:Basic.__eq__ and sympy/core/sympify.py:_sympify — related (safer) behavior: Basic.__eq__ uses _sympify (which is sympify(..., strict=True)) and therefore does not reach the repr-parsing fallback. Evidence: Basic.__eq__ calls "other = _sympify(other)" and _sympify is implemented as "return sympify(a, strict=True)". Consequence: there is an inconsistency between Expr.__eq__ (which uses non-strict sympify) and Basic.__eq__ (which uses strict sympification), and the risky behavior is exercised by Expr.

Note: sympify's docstring already warns that it uses eval and should not be used on unsanitized input; nevertheless, Expr.__eq__ calls the non-strict sympify pathway allowing repr-derived strings to be parsed and evaluated.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Comparing a SymPy expression (e.g. Symbol('x')) to an unrelated Python object must not execute code derived from that object's __repr__. A plain equality comparison with a non-SymPy object should not parse/evaluate that object's repr and should yield False (or otherwise avoid executing arbitrary repr strings).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Expr.__eq__ invokes sympify on the other operand; sympify's fallback path stringifies arbitrary objects and passes that text through the parser/evaluator, causing evaluation of repr-derived code.     expressions, and tries to simplify it. The primary metric is the
    total degree. Some attempts are made to choose the simplest possible

    very slow (see the ``quick=True`` option).

    denominator together, this function just brings numerator and denominator
    into a canonical form. This is much faster, but has potentially worse
    results. However, if the input is a polynomial, then the result is
    guaranteed to be an equivalent polynomial of minimal degree.

    following:

    - a function
    - an iterable of the form (func, var1, var2, ...)
    - anything else, interpreted as a generator

    A function is used to indicate that said function is likely to occur in a
    simplified expression.

from __future__ import print_function, division

from sympy.core import S, Add, Expr, Basic, Mul
from sympy.assumptions import Q, ask

def refine(expr, assumptions=True):
    """
    Simplify an expression using assumptions.

    Gives the form of expr that would be obtained if symbols
    in it were replaced by explicit numerical expressions satisfying
    the assumptions.

    Examples
    ========

        >>> from sympy import refine, sqrt, Q
        >>> from sympy.abc import x
        >>> refine(sqrt(x**2), Q.real(x))
        Abs(x)
        >>> refine(sqrt(x**2), Q.positive(x))
        x

    """
    if not isinstance(expr, Basic):
        return expr
    if not expr.is_Atom:
        args = [refine(arg, assumptions) for arg in expr.args]
        # TODO: this will probably not work with Integral or Polynomial
        expr = expr.func(*args)
    if hasattr(expr, '_eval_refine'):
        ref_expr = expr._eval_refine(assumptions)
        if ref_expr is not None:
            return ref_expr
    name = expr.__class__.__name__
    handler = handlers_dict.get(name, None)
    if handler is None:
        return expr
    new_expr = handler(expr, assumptions)
    if (new_expr is None) or (expr == new_expr):
        return expr
    if not isinstance(new_expr, Expr):
        return new_expr
    return refine(new_expr, assumptions)


def refine_abs(expr, assumptions):
    """
    Handler for the absolute value.

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy import Symbol, Q, refine, Abs
    >>> from sympy.assumptions.refine import refine_abs
    >>> from sympy.abc import x
    >>> refine_abs(Abs(x), Q.real(x))
    >>> refine_abs(Abs(x), Q.positive(x))
    x
    >>> refine_abs(Abs(x), Q.negative(x))
    -x

    """
    from sympy.core.logic import fuzzy_not
    from sympy import Abs
    arg = expr.args[0]
    if ask(Q.real(arg), assumptions) and \
            fuzzy_not(ask(Q.negative(arg), assumptions)):
        # if it's nonnegative
        return arg
    if ask(Q.negative(arg), assumptions):
        return -arg
    # arg is Mul
    if isinstance(arg, Mul):
        r = [refine(abs(a), assumptions) for a in arg.args]
        non_abs = []
        in_abs = []
        for i in r:
            if isinstance(i, Abs):
                in_abs.append(i.args[0])
            else:
                non_abs.append(i)
        return Mul(*non_abs) * Abs(Mul(*in_abs))


def refine_Pow(expr, assumptions):
    """
    Handler for instances of Pow.

    >>> from sympy import Symbol, Q
    >>> from sympy.assumptions.refine import refine_Pow
    >>> from sympy.abc import x,y,z
    >>> refine_Pow((-1)**x, Q.real(x))
    >>> refine_Pow((-1)**x, Q.even(x))
    1
    >>> refine_Pow((-1)**x, Q.odd(x))
    -1

    For powers of -1, even parts of the exponent can be simplified:

    >>> refine_Pow((-1)**(x+y), Q.even(x))
    (-1)**y
    >>> refine_Pow((-1)**(x+y+z), Q.odd(x) & Q.odd(z))
    (-1)**y
    >>> refine_Pow((-1)**(x+y+2), Q.odd(x))
    (-1)**(y + 1)
    >>> refine_Pow((-1)**(x+3), True)
    (-1)**(x + 1)

    """
    from sympy.core import Pow, Rational
    from sympy.functions.elementary.complexes import Abs
    from sympy.functions import sign
    if isinstance(expr.base, Abs):
        if ask(Q.real(expr.base.args[0]), assumptions) and \
                ask(Q.even(expr.exp), assumptions):
            return expr.base.args[0] ** expr.exp
    if ask(Q.real(expr.base), assumptions):
        if expr.base.is_number:
            if ask(Q.even(expr.exp), assumptions):
                return abs(expr.base) ** expr.exp
            if ask(Q.odd(expr.exp), assumptions):
                return sign(expr.base) * abs(expr.base) ** expr.exp
        if isinstance(expr.exp, Rational):
            if type(expr.base) is Pow:
                return abs(expr.base.base) ** (expr.base.exp * expr.exp)

        if expr.base is S.NegativeOne:
            if expr.exp.is_Add:

                old = expr

                # For powers of (-1) we can remove
                #  - even terms
                #  - pairs of odd terms
                #  - a single odd term + 1
                #  - A numerical constant N can be replaced with mod(N,2)

                coeff, terms = expr.exp.as_coeff_add()
                terms = set(terms)
                even_terms = set([])
                odd_terms = set([])
                initial_number_of_terms = len(terms)

                for t in terms:
                    if ask(Q.even(t), assumptions):
                        even_terms.add(t)
                    elif ask(Q.odd(t), assumptions):
                        odd_terms.add(t)

                terms -= even_terms
                if len(odd_terms) % 2:
                    terms -= odd_terms
                    new_coeff = (coeff + S.One) % 2
                else:
                    terms -= odd_terms
                    new_coeff = coeff % 2

                if new_coeff != coeff or len(terms) < initial_number_of_terms:
                    terms.add(new_coeff)
                    expr = expr.base**(Add(*terms))

                e2 = 2*expr.exp
                if ask(Q.even(e2), assumptions):

                        e2 *= expr.base

                        if ask(Q.integer(p.exp), assumptions):
                            i = (i + 1)/2
                            if ask(Q.even(i), assumptions):

                            elif ask(Q.odd(i), assumptions):

                            else:

def refine_atan2(expr, assumptions):
    """
    Handler for the atan2 function

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy import Symbol, Q, refine, atan2
    >>> from sympy.assumptions.refine import refine_atan2
    >>> from sympy.abc import x, y
    >>> refine_atan2(atan2(y,x), Q.real(y) & Q.positive(x))
    atan(y/x)
    >>> refine_atan2(atan2(y,x), Q.negative(y) & Q.negative(x))
    atan(y/x) - pi
    >>> refine_atan2(atan2(y,x), Q.positive(y) & Q.negative(x))
    atan(y/x) + pi
    >>> refine_atan2(atan2(y,x), Q.zero(y) & Q.negative(x))
    pi
    >>> refine_atan2(atan2(y,x), Q.positive(y) & Q.zero(x))
    pi/2
    >>> refine_atan2(atan2(y,x), Q.negative(y) & Q.zero(x))
    -pi/2
    >>> refine_atan2(atan2(y,x), Q.zero(y) & Q.zero(x))
    nan
    """
    from sympy.functions.elementary.trigonometric import atan
    from sympy.core import S
    y, x = expr.args
    if ask(Q.real(y) & Q.positive(x), assumptions):
        return atan(y / x)
    elif ask(Q.negative(y) & Q.negative(x), assumptions):
        return atan(y / x) - S.Pi
    elif ask(Q.positive(y) & Q.negative(x), assumptions):
        return atan(y / x) + S.Pi
    elif ask(Q.zero(y) & Q.negative(x), assumptions):
        return S.Pi
    elif ask(Q.positive(y) & Q.zero(x), assumptions):
        return S.Pi/2
    elif ask(Q.negative(y) & Q.zero(x), assumptions):
        return -S.Pi/2
    elif ask(Q.zero(y) & Q.zero(x), assumptions):
        return S.NaN
    else:
        return expr

def isqrt(n):
    """Return the largest integer less than or equal to sqrt(n)."""
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n must be nonnegative")
    n = int(n)

    # Fast path: with IEEE 754 binary64 floats and a correctly-rounded
    # math.sqrt, int(math.sqrt(n)) works for any integer n satisfying 0 <= n <
    # 4503599761588224 = 2**52 + 2**27. But Python doesn't guarantee either
    # IEEE 754 format floats *or* correct rounding of math.sqrt, so check the
    # answer and fall back to the slow method if necessary.
    if n < 4503599761588224:

        if 0 <= n - s*s <= 2*s:
            return s

    return integer_nthroot(n, 2)[0]

    Return a tuple containing x = floor(y**(1/n))
    and a boolean indicating whether the result is exact (that is,
    whether x**n == y).

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy import integer_nthroot
    >>> integer_nthroot(16, 2)
    (4, True)
    >>> integer_nthroot(26, 2)
    (5, False)

    function should be used:

    >>> from sympy.ntheory.primetest import is_square
    >>> is_square(26)
    False

    ========

    integer_log

        raise ValueError("y must be nonnegative")
    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError("n must be positive")

    if n == 1:

    # avoid overflow

            guess = int(2.0**(exp - shift) + 1) << shift
        else:
            guess = int(2.0**exp)
    if guess > 2**50:
        # Newton iteration
        xprev, x = -1, guess
        while 1:
            t = x**(n - 1)
            xprev, x = x, ((n - 1)*x + y//t)//n
            if abs(x - xprev) < 2:

        x = guess
    # Compensate
    t = x**n
    while t < y:
        x += 1
        t = x**n
    while t > y:
        x -= 1
        t = x**n
    return int(x), t == y  # int converts long to int if possible

    such that :math:`|y| \geq |x^e|` and ``bool`` is True if $y = x^e$.

    >>> from sympy import integer_log
    >>> integer_log(125, 5)
    (3, True)
    >>> integer_log(17, 9)
    (1, False)

    (2, True)
    >>> integer_log(-125,-5)
    (3, True)

    sympy.ntheory.factor_.multiplicity
    sympy.ntheory.factor_.perfect_power

    if x == 1:
        raise ValueError('x cannot take value as 1')

    x = as_int(x)
    y = as_int(y)
    r = e = 0

        while y >= d:

            r = r or rem
            e += m
            if y > d:
                d *= d

  - Why I looked: the draft claimed Pow._eval_power is used to denest nested powers; Pow.__new__ is the place that calls _eval_power during construction.
  - What I expected to learn: whether Pow.__new__ calls b._eval_power(e) and whether the return value is accepted unconditionally (non-None return used as denest).
  - Code evidence: In sympy/core/power.py, Pow.__new__ contains:
    - lines 301-304: obj = b._eval_power(e) ; if obj is not None: return obj
  - Analysis: this confirms that denesting can occur at construction time — i.e., when a Pow is constructed (e.g. sqrt(sin(x)**2)), the base's _eval_power is consulted and any non-None return is accepted as the constructed object. So denesting does not only happen in powsimp/powdenest — it can happen earlier during expression construction.

- Pow._eval_power (sympy/core/power.py)
  - Why I looked: the draft points to this method as the core location performing a denest that can be unsafe for complex bases.
  - What I expected to learn: whether code computes a multiplicative phase s, whether it returns s*Pow(b, e*other), and whether it has an explicit guard requiring the inner base be real before denesting for the (b**even)**(1/2) pattern.
  - Code evidence:
    - The method begins at line 332.
    - There are helper functions _half and _n2 at lines 345-361 that detect half exponents (denominator 2) and evaluate numeric closeness.
    - The branch that handles real/extended-real exponents and computes s is present (see lines 363-411).
    - The specific _half(other) path computes s using exp(2*pi*I*other*floor(...)) at lines 389-391 and then normalizes s at lines 392-395.
    - If s is not None the method returns s*Pow(b, e*other) at lines 412-413.
    - There is an earlier special-case for e.is_even where b may be replaced by abs(b) if b.is_extended_real (lines 375-379), but there is no blanket check that denies the denest unless b.is_extended_real is True before computing s and returning s*Pow(...).
  - Analysis: the code indeed computes a multiplicative phase s for half exponents and can return s*Pow(b, e*other). There is no explicit short-circuit guard of the form "if e.is_even and _half(other) and b.is_extended_real is not True: return None" present in this version of the file. Therefore the claim that Pow._eval_power may denest (b**even)**(1/2) to b for non-real b is supported.

- powsimp._denest_pow (sympy/simplify/powsimp.py)
  - Why I looked: the draft claims powsimp/_denest_pow trusts Pow._eval_power return value and propagates unsafe denests to higher-level simplifiers.
  - What I expected: find where _denest_pow calls b._eval_power(e) and how it uses the return value.
  - Code evidence:
    - In sympy/simplify/powsimp.py, function _denest_pow begins at line 594.
    - Lines 603-609: b, e = eq.as_base_exp(); if b.is_Pow ...: new = b._eval_power(e); if new is not None: eq = new; b, e = new.as_base_exp()
  - Analysis: this confirms _denest_pow accepts any non-None return value from b._eval_power(e) and uses it as the denested expression. There is no additional check here to ensure the denest is only applied when the base is real.

- trigsimp (sympy/simplify/trigsimp.py)
  - Why I looked: the draft claims trigsimp triggers the pow-denest path and presents an incorrect simplification cos(x) + sin(x).
  - What I expected: verify whether trigsimp directly calls powdenest or relies on other simplifiers that can perform denesting.
  - Code evidence and analysis:
    - trigsimp.py is large and contains many different routines. A search of trigsimp.py did not find direct calls to powdenest or powsimp (no matches for 'powdenest' or 'powsimp(' in trigsimp.py).
    - However, because Pow.__new__ calls b._eval_power(e) at construction time, denesting can already happen when the subexpression sqrt(sin(x)**2) is constructed, before any trigsimp-specific logic runs.
    - In addition, other parts of the simplification pipeline that trigsimp triggers or that user code commonly uses (for example, powdenest/powsimp invoked elsewhere) will also accept the denest from Pow._eval_power and propagate it.
  - Conclusion: the user-visible incorrect result (cos(x) + sin(x)) can appear when trigsimp is run, but the root cause is the denest capability in Pow._eval_power (propagated either via Pow.__new__ at construction time, or via powsimp/powdenest later). The draft's statement that "trigsimp triggers the above pow-denest path" is generally true in effect (trigsimp is a common entry point where users notice the simplification), but its implication that trigsimp itself contains a direct call to powdenest is not supported. The correct statement is: trigsimp can present the wrong result because the simplification pipeline and/or expression construction call into Pow._eval_power (and powsimp._denest_pow also accepts its return), allowing unsafe denesting to propagate to trigsimp's output.

bug_report.Title: trigsimp incorrectly denests sqrt(sin(x)**2) to sin(x) for general (complex) x
bug_report.Description: trigsimp (via the power-denesting pipeline and/or expression construction) simplifies cos(x) + sqrt(sin(x)**2) to cos(x) + sin(x) when x is not assumed real. This simplification is incorrect for general complex x because the principal square root of z**2 is not equal to z for arbitrary complex z.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Overly-permissive denesting assumption in Pow._eval_power (sympy/core/power.py: class Pow, method _eval_power): the method computes a multiplicative phase and may return s*Pow(b, e*other) for nested powers, which allows (b**(even))**(1/2) to be turned into b (or s*b) without requiring the inner base b to be known real. The implementation includes a helper _half and computes s via an expression like exp(2*pi*I*other*floor(...)) and then returns s*Pow(b, e*other) when s is not None (see sympy/core/power.py lines ~345-395 and 412-413).

2) Denest can occur at Pow construction time (sympy/core/power.py: Pow.__new__): when a Pow is constructed the code calls b._eval_power(e) and accepts any non-None return as the constructed object (sympy/core/power.py lines ~301-304). That means sqrt(sin(x)**2) may be denested to sin(x) as the Pow object is built, before any higher-level simplifiers run.

3) powsimp/_denest_pow trusts Pow._eval_power's return value (sympy/simplify/powsimp.py: function _denest_pow): _denest_pow calls new = b._eval_power(e) and, if new is not None, replaces the expression with new (sympy/simplify/powsimp.py lines ~603-609). Any unsafe denest returned by Pow._eval_power therefore propagates through the powdenest/powsimp pipeline.

4) The symptom is exposed in trigsimp outputs (sympy/simplify/trigsimp.py): users observing trigsimp(cos(x) + sqrt(sin(x)**2)) may see cos(x) + sin(x). Trigsimp itself does not need to call powdenest explicitly for the user-visible incorrect simplification to appear, because the unsafe denest may already have occurred at Pow construction time or may be applied by other callers of Pow._eval_power (for example, powdenest/powsimp). Thus trigsimp's result can reflect the unsafe denest originating in Pow._eval_power and propagated by powdenest.

5) Correct / conservative relationship for safe denesting (preserved from investigation): when attempting to denest (b**(even))**(1/2) to b, the denest must only be allowed if the inner base is known real. The investigation identifies the exact guard used to diagnose the defect (this expresses the necessary conservatism):

    if e.is_even and _half(other) and b.is_extended_real is not True:
        return None

Returning None from _eval_power is the established signal to callers that no special-case denest is safe; callers (Pow.__new__ and _denest_pow) treat a None return as 'do not denest'.

Investigation gap: the code path that computes s (via floor/arg expressions) can under some symbolic circumstances evaluate to s == 1 and thereby permit the denest for symbolic b (e.g. b = sin(x)). The investigation verified the computation exists but did not produce a concrete step-by-step trace showing exactly how s became 1 for sin(x) in the failing run. That gap remains.
StepsToReproduce: Start a Python session with SymPy imported.
Create an unconstrained symbol: x = symbols('x')
Evaluate trigsimp(cos(x) + sqrt(sin(x)**2)) and observe the result.
(Optional) Repeat with x = symbols('x', real=True) and evaluate trigsimp(cos(x) + sqrt(sin(x)**2)) to compare behavior.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: For an unconstrained symbol x (complex by default), trigsimp(cos(x) + sqrt(sin(x)**2)) should not simplify sqrt(sin(x)**2) to sin(x); the expression should remain cos(x) + sqrt(sin(x)**2) (or an equivalent form that preserves branch information). When x is declared real, trigsimp may use the real-valued simplification and yield cos(x) + Abs(sin(x)) (or an equivalent correct real-case simplification).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: For an unconstrained symbol x, trigsimp(cos(x) + sqrt(sin(x)**2)) simplifies to cos(x) + sin(x), incorrectly removing the principal-square-root branch information and assuming sqrt(z**2) == z for general complex z.

``eq`` should be an homogeneous expression of degree two in three variables
    and it is assumed to be zero.

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy.abc import x, y, z
    >>> from sympy.solvers.diophantine import diop_ternary_quadratic
    >>> diop_ternary_quadratic(x**2 + 3*y**2 - z**2)
    (1, 0, 1)
    >>> diop_ternary_quadratic(4*x**2 + 5*y**2 - z**2)
    (1, 0, 2)
    >>> diop_ternary_quadratic(45*x**2 - 7*y**2 - 8*x*y - z**2)
    (28, 45, 105)
    >>> diop_ternary_quadratic(x**2 - 49*y**2 - z**2 + 13*z*y -8*x*y)
    (9, 1, 5)
    """
    var, coeff, diop_type = classify_diop(eq, _dict=False)

    if diop_type in (
            "homogeneous_ternary_quadratic",
            "homogeneous_ternary_quadratic_normal"):
        return _diop_ternary_quadratic(var, coeff)


def _diop_ternary_quadratic(_var, coeff):

    x, y, z = _var
    var = [x, y, z]

    # Equations of the form B*x*y + C*z*x + E*y*z = 0 and At least two of the
    # coefficients A, B, C are non-zero.
    # There are infinitely many solutions for the equation.
    # Ex: (0, 0, t), (0, t, 0), (t, 0, 0)
    # Equation can be re-written as y*(B*x + E*z) = -C*x*z and we can find rather
    # unobvious solutions. Set y = -C and B*x + E*z = x*z. The latter can be solved by
    # using methods for binary quadratic diophantine equations. Let's select the
    # solution which minimizes |x| + |z|

    if not any(coeff[i**2] for i in var):
        if coeff[x*z]:
            sols = diophantine(coeff[x*y]*x + coeff[y*z]*z - x*z)
            s = sols.pop()
            min_sum = abs(s[0]) + abs(s[1])

            for r in sols:
                m = abs(r[0]) + abs(r[1])
                if m < min_sum:
                    s = r
                    min_sum = m

            x_0, y_0, z_0 = _remove_gcd(s[0], -coeff[x*z], s[1])

        else:
            var[0], var[1] = _var[1], _var[0]
            y_0, x_0, z_0 = _diop_ternary_quadratic(var, coeff)

        return x_0, y_0, z_0

    if coeff[x**2] == 0:
        # If the coefficient of x is zero change the variables
        if coeff[y**2] == 0:
            var[0], var[2] = _var[2], _var[0]
            z_0, y_0, x_0 = _diop_ternary_quadratic(var, coeff)

    assert classify_diop(x*y + z + w + x**2) == (

    assert classify_diop(x*y + z*w) == (
        [w, x, y, z], {x*y: 1, w*z: 1}, 'homogeneous_general_quadratic')
    assert classify_diop(x*y**2 + 1) == (

bug_report.Title: diophantine returns incomplete / order-dependent results when permute=True (permute not propagated)
bug_report.Description: Calling diophantine(..., permute=True) can produce different and incomplete solution sets depending on the order of the syms argument because internal calls to diophantine() do not forward the caller's permute flag and therefore use the default permute=False.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Omitted permute in syms-remapping branch (sympy/solvers/diophantine.py : diophantine): when syms is supplied and differs from the function's internal variable ordering the code remaps tuples returned by an inner call to diophantine(eq, param). That inner call is invoked as diophantine(eq, param) with no permute argument (i.e. permute defaults to False), so the base solutions lack the permutations requested by the top-level caller. The correct relationship for consistent behavior is that the inner call should be invoked with the outer permute setting (for example: diophantine(eq, param, permute=permute)).

2) Omitted permute in numerator/denominator handling (sympy/solvers/diophantine.py : diophantine): when eq has a non-trivial denominator the code computes dsol = diophantine(d) and good = diophantine(n) - dsol. Both diophantine(d) and diophantine(n) are invoked without a permute argument and therefore use permute=False. Using non-permuted subresults for subtraction/filtering when the top-level call requested permute=True can remove valid solutions. The correct relationship is that these internal diophantine calls should receive the caller's permute flag (e.g. diophantine(d, permute=permute) and diophantine(n, permute=permute)).

3) Omitted permute in helper used by ternary quadratic solving (sympy/solvers/diophantine.py : _diop_ternary_quadratic): the helper calls diophantine(...) (for example sols = diophantine(coeff[x*y]*x + coeff[y*z]*z - x*z)) without a permute argument, again defaulting to permute=False. This is a separate consistency gap: top-level permute=True does not influence this helper-level call. The location is identified as a related finding and encodes the same incorrect assumption (that internal diophantine invocations need not inherit the top-level permute setting).
StepsToReproduce: In a SymPy REPL or script, define symbols m, n and run: diophantine(n**4 + m**4 - 2**4 - 3**4, syms=(m,n), permute=True)
Then run: diophantine(n**4 + m**4 - 2**4 - 3**4, syms=(n,m), permute=True)
Compare the two results; they differ (one is missing permutations).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: diophantine(..., permute=True) should return the same complete set of permuted solutions regardless of the order of the syms argument (for the example n**4 + m**4 - 2**4 - 3**4 both syms=(m,n) and syms=(n,m) should produce the same full set of 8 ordered pairs).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: For the example: diophantine(n**4 + m**4 - 2**4 - 3**4, syms=(m,n), permute=True) returns {(-3, -2), (-3, 2), (-2, -3), (-2, 3), (2, -3), (2, 3), (3, -2), (3, 2)} while diophantine(n**4 + m**4 - 2**4 - 3**4, syms=(n,m), permute=True) returns {(3, 2)} — the second result is missing the other permutations.

def _discrete_log_trial_mul(n, a, b, order=None):
    """
    Trial multiplication algorithm for computing the discrete logarithm of
    ``a`` to the base ``b`` modulo ``n``.

    The algorithm finds the discrete logarithm using exhaustive search. This
    naive method is used as fallback algorithm of ``discrete_log`` when the
    group order is very small.

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy.ntheory.residue_ntheory import _discrete_log_trial_mul
    >>> _discrete_log_trial_mul(41, 15, 7)
    3

    See Also
    ========

    discrete_log

    References
    ==========

    .. [1] "Handbook of applied cryptography", Menezes, A. J., Van, O. P. C., &
        Vanstone, S. A. (1997).
    """
    a %= n
    b %= n
    if order is None:
        order = n
    x = 1
    for i in range(order):
        if x == a:
            return i
        x = x * b % n
    raise ValueError("Log does not exist")


def _discrete_log_shanks_steps(n, a, b, order=None):
    """
    Baby-step giant-step algorithm for computing the discrete logarithm of
    ``a`` to the base ``b`` modulo ``n``.

    The algorithm is a time-memory trade-off of the method of exhaustive
    search. It uses `O(sqrt(m))` memory, where `m` is the group order.

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy.ntheory.residue_ntheory import _discrete_log_shanks_steps
    >>> _discrete_log_shanks_steps(41, 15, 7)
    3

    See Also
    ========

    discrete_log

    References
    ==========

    .. [1] "Handbook of applied cryptography", Menezes, A. J., Van, O. P. C., &
        Vanstone, S. A. (1997).
    """
    a %= n
    b %= n
    if order is None:
        order = n_order(b, n)
    m = isqrt(order) + 1
    T = dict()
    x = 1
    for i in range(m):
        T[x] = i
        x = x * b % n
    z = mod_inverse(b, n)
    z = pow(z, m, n)
    x = a
    for i in range(m):
        if x in T:
            return i * m + T[x]
        x = x * z % n
    raise ValueError("Log does not exist")

4. If a is an instance of ``Pow`` then two cases arise as following:

        - If a is of type (symbol_indep)**(symbol_dep) then the remainder is
          evaluated with the help of discrete_log function and then the least
          period is being found out with the help of totient function.
          period*n + remainder is the required solution in this case.
          For reference: (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler's_theorem)

        - If a is of type (symbol_dep)**(symbol_indep) then we try to find all
          primitive solutions list with the help of nthroot_mod function.
          m*n + rem is the general solution where rem belongs to solutions list
          from nthroot_mod function.

    Parameters
    ==========

    modterm, rhs : Expr
        The modular equation to be inverted, ``modterm - rhs = 0``

    symbol : Symbol
        The variable in the equation to be inverted.

    n : Dummy
        Dummy variable for output g_n.

    Returns
    =======

    A tuple (f_x, g_n) is being returned where f_x is modular independent function
    of symbol and g_n being set of values f_x can have.

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy import symbols, exp, Mod, Dummy, S
    >>> from sympy.solvers.solveset import _invert_modular as invert_modular
    >>> x, y = symbols('x y')
    >>> n = Dummy('n')
    >>> invert_modular(Mod(exp(x), 7), S(5), n, x)

    >>> invert_modular(Mod(x, 7), S(5), n, x)
    (x, ImageSet(Lambda(_n, 7*_n + 5), Integers))
    >>> invert_modular(Mod(3*x + 8, 7), S(5), n, x)
    (x, ImageSet(Lambda(_n, 7*_n + 6), Integers))
    >>> invert_modular(Mod(x**4, 7), S(5), n, x)
    (x, EmptySet)
    >>> invert_modular(Mod(2**(x**2 + x + 1), 7), S(2), n, x)
    (x**2 + x + 1, ImageSet(Lambda(_n, 3*_n + 1), Naturals0))

    """

            for term in list(_term_factors(a))):
        # Check for complex arguments
        return modterm, rhs

    if abs(rhs) >= abs(m):
        # if rhs has value greater than value of m.
        return symbol, EmptySet

    if a == symbol:
        return symbol, ImageSet(Lambda(n, m*n + rhs), S.Integers)

    if a.is_Add:
        # g + h = a
        g, h = a.as_independent(symbol)
        if g is not S.Zero:
            x_indep_term = rhs - Mod(g, m)
            return _invert_modular(Mod(h, m), Mod(x_indep_term, m), n, symbol)

    if a.is_Mul:

        g, h = a.as_independent(symbol)

            x_indep_term = rhs*invert(g, m)
            return _invert_modular(Mod(h, m), Mod(x_indep_term, m), n, symbol)

    if a.is_Pow:
        # base**expo = a
        base, expo = a.args

            # m, rhs are made coprime by dividing igcd(m, rhs)
            try:
                remainder = discrete_log(m / igcd(m, rhs), rhs, a.base)
            except ValueError:  # log does not exist
                return modterm, rhs

            # the least period of expo in which it is repeats itself.
            # (a**(totient(m)) - 1) divides m. Here is link of theorem:
            # (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler's_theorem)
            period = totient(m)
            for p in divisors(period):
                # there might a lesser period exist than totient(m).
                if pow(a.base, p, m / igcd(m, a.base)) == 1:

            # not smart enough to handle infinite rhs as here expo has infinite
            # rhs = ImageSet(Lambda(n, period*n + remainder), S.Naturals0).

def ilcm(*args):
    """Computes integer least common multiple.

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy.core.numbers import ilcm
    >>> ilcm(5, 10)
    10
    >>> ilcm(7, 3)
    21
    >>> ilcm(5, 10, 15)
    30

    """
    if len(args) < 2:
        raise TypeError(
            'ilcm() takes at least 2 arguments (%s given)' % len(args))
    if 0 in args:
        return 0
    a = args[0]
    for b in args[1:]:
        a = a // igcd(a, b) * b # since gcd(a,b) | a
    return a


def igcdex(a, b):
    """Returns x, y, g such that g = x*a + y*b = gcd(a, b).

       >>> from sympy.core.numbers import igcdex
       >>> igcdex(2, 3)
       (-1, 1, 1)
       >>> igcdex(10, 12)
       (-1, 1, 2)

       >>> x, y, g = igcdex(100, 2004)
       >>> x, y, g
       (-20, 1, 4)
       >>> x*100 + y*2004
       4

    """
    if (not a) and (not b):
        return (0, 1, 0)

    if not a:
        return (0, b//abs(b), abs(b))
    if not b:
        return (a//abs(a), 0, abs(a))

    if a < 0:
        a, x_sign = -a, -1
    else:
        x_sign = 1

    if b < 0:
        b, y_sign = -b, -1
    else:
        y_sign = 1

    x, y, r, s = 1, 0, 0, 1

    while b:
        (c, q) = (a % b, a // b)
        (a, b, r, s, x, y) = (b, c, x - q*r, y - q*s, r, s)

    return (x*x_sign, y*y_sign, a)

    a ValueError is raised.

    >>> from sympy.core.numbers import mod_inverse

    3 modulo 11. This is the same as finding x such

- Fix strategy: add an explicit early check for a % p == 0 in nthroot_mod (public entry) and for s % p == 0 at the start of _nthroot_mod1; return 0 (or [0] when all_roots=True). Apply to both places so internal callers and the public API are safe.
- Hardcoded constants: no numeric constants need to change; the issue is a missing conditional, not a wrong constant. Multiplicative-group constants (p-1, q dividing p-1) remain correct but must not be used for the zero residue.
- New/overridden methods: none. Only small guards added to existing functions. Add unit tests (see LOW_LEVEL).
- Investigation gaps: the agent did not trace discrete_log with a concrete zero input (did not run or simulate discrete_log(…, 0, …)) to show the exact failure mode; tests were not executed to confirm behavior after the change. These should be validated in CI/tests.

- **Wrong assumption**: Public nthroot_mod proceeds to multiplicative-group algorithms for prime p without treating a % p == 0 as a special case.

- Why I checked: The draft claims the public nthroot_mod lacks a short-circuit for a % p == 0 and therefore omits the trivial root.

bug_report.Title: nthroot_mod omits trivial root x ≡ 0 (mod p) when input reaches multiplicative-group branch with a % p == 0
bug_report.Description: When solving x**n ≡ a (mod p) with a ≡ 0 (mod p), the implementation path that uses multiplicative-group algorithms does not treat the zero residue as a special case. In particular, when nthroot_mod delegates to the helper that assumes residues are units, the trivial solution x ≡ 0 (mod p) can be omitted or an error can be raised instead of returning the zero root. Example context: calling nthroot_mod with inputs that cause the function to take the branch that directly calls _nthroot_mod1 (i.e., when (p - 1) % n == 0) while a % p == 0 can lead to this problem.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) nthroot_mod (sympy/ntheory/residue_ntheory.py::nthroot_mod) has no global short-circuit for a % p == 0 and may dispatch directly into multiplicative-group code when (p - 1) % n == 0 (see lines 774–781). In that dispatch case the public entry point forwards s == a into routines that assume a unit, so the trivial residue x ≡ 0 (mod p) is not handled at the public-entry branch point.

2) _nthroot_mod1 (sympy/ntheory/residue_ntheory.py::_nthroot_mod1) assumes its input s is a unit (s % p != 0). It computes r1 = pow(s, x, p) and s1 = pow(s, f, p) and then calls discrete_log(p, s1, h) (lines 725–728) without first checking or reducing s modulo p to detect s == 0. If s % p == 0 then s1 == 0 and discrete_log is invoked with a == 0 (invalid in the multiplicative group), which causes the discrete-log routines to fail to find an exponent and raise ValueError("Log does not exist"). This is the immediate code-level cause for omission/error in that branch.

3) _nthroot_mod2 (sympy/ntheory/residue_ntheory.py::_nthroot_mod2) forwards intermediate s values into repeated calls to _nthroot_mod1 (lines 690–697). Because _nthroot_mod1 assumes a nonzero residue, passing s == 0 into _nthroot_mod2 will propagate the invalid assumption and surface the same failure mode.

4) Related APIs treat zero as a valid right-hand side: is_nthpow_residue returns True when a % m == 0 (sympy/ntheory/residue_ntheory.py::is_nthpow_residue, line 641), and the square-root routines explicitly handle a % p == 0 (sqrt_mod_iter reduces a mod p and calls the zero-case branch; lines 322–326). This creates an API inconsistency: some predicates and routines accept a == 0, while the multiplicative-group branch used by nthroot_mod/_nthroot_mod1 assumes nonzero residues.

5) Test-suite gap: tests exercise many nthroot_mod cases but do not include an explicit assertion that nthroot_mod(a, n, p) (or nthroot_mod(..., all_roots=True)) returns 0 (or [0]) when a % p == 0. The absence of such tests allowed the missing-zero behavior in the multiplicative-group path to go unchecked (see sympy/ntheory/tests/test_residue.py where nthroot_mod is tested but the a % p == 0 case is not asserted explicitly).
StepsToReproduce: In a Python REPL or test file, from sympy.ntheory.residue_ntheory import nthroot_mod

Call nthroot_mod with inputs that cause (p - 1) % n == 0 and where a % p == 0 (these inputs exercise the multiplicative-group branch). Observe the function proceeds into multiplicative-group code and does not return the trivial root 0 (it may raise a ValueError from discrete_log).
More generally, call nthroot_mod(a, n, p) and nthroot_mod(a, n, p, True) for a values divisible by p and verify whether 0 (or [0]) appears in the result.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: User-visible contract: whenever a % p == 0, the congruence x**n ≡ a (mod p) has the trivial solution x ≡ 0 (mod p); nthroot_mod(a, n, p) should return 0 and nthroot_mod(a, n, p, all_roots=True) should include [0] among the returned roots. Related predicates such as is_nthpow_residue should remain consistent (they already return True for a % p == 0).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: In the code path that uses multiplicative-group routines (_nthroot_mod1), a input divisible by p (s % p == 0) is not recognized as the zero residue prior to calling primitive_root/discrete_log. This leads discrete_log to be invoked with a == 0 (a value not in the multiplicative group modulo a prime), causing the discrete-log search to fail (ValueError) or otherwise preventing the trivial solution x ≡ 0 (mod p) from being returned. The issue is triggered when nthroot_mod dispatches to _nthroot_mod1 (i.e., when (p - 1) % n == 0).

import inspect
from sympy.core.cache import cacheit
from sympy.core.singleton import S
from sympy.core.sympify import _sympify
from sympy.logic.boolalg import Boolean

class AssumptionsContext(set):
    """Set representing assumptions.

    This is used to represent global assumptions, but you can also use this
    class to create your own local assumptions contexts. It is basically a thin
    wrapper to Python's set, so see its documentation for advanced usage.

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy import AppliedPredicate, Q
    >>> from sympy.assumptions.assume import global_assumptions
    >>> global_assumptions
    AssumptionsContext()
    >>> from sympy.abc import x
    >>> global_assumptions.add(Q.real(x))
    >>> global_assumptions
    AssumptionsContext({Q.real(x)})
    >>> global_assumptions.remove(Q.real(x))
    >>> global_assumptions
    AssumptionsContext()
    >>> global_assumptions.clear()

    """

    def add(self, *assumptions):
        """Add an assumption."""
        for a in assumptions:
            super(AssumptionsContext, self).add(a)

    def _sympystr(self, printer):
        if not self:
            return "%s()" % self.__class__.__name__
        return "%s(%s)" % (self.__class__.__name__, printer._print_set(self))

global_assumptions = AssumptionsContext()


class AppliedPredicate(Boolean):
    """The class of expressions resulting from applying a Predicate.

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy import Q, Symbol
    >>> x = Symbol('x')
    >>> Q.integer(x)
    Q.integer(x)
    >>> type(Q.integer(x))
    <class 'sympy.assumptions.assume.AppliedPredicate'>

    """
    __slots__ = ()

    def __new__(cls, predicate, arg):
        arg = _sympify(arg)
        return Boolean.__new__(cls, predicate, arg)

    is_Atom = True  # do not attempt to decompose this

    @property
    def arg(self):
        """
        Return the expression used by this assumption.

        Examples
        ========

        >>> from sympy import Q, Symbol
        >>> x = Symbol('x')
        >>> a = Q.integer(x + 1)
        >>> a.arg
        x + 1

        """
        return self._args[1]

    @property
    def args(self):
        return self._args[1:]

    @property
    def func(self):
        return self._args[0]

    @cacheit
    def sort_key(self, order=None):
        return (self.class_key(), (2, (self.func.name, self.arg.sort_key())),
                S.One.sort_key(), S.One)

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if type(other) is AppliedPredicate:
            return self._args == other._args
        return False

    def __hash__(self):
        return super(AppliedPredicate, self).__hash__()

    def _eval_ask(self, assumptions):
        return self.func.eval(self.arg, assumptions)

    @property
    def binary_symbols(self):
        from sympy.core.relational import Eq, Ne
        if self.func.name in ['is_true', 'is_false']:
            i = self.arg
            if i.is_Boolean or i.is_Symbol or isinstance(i, (Eq, Ne)):
                return i.binary_symbols
        return set()


class Predicate(Boolean):
    """A predicate is a function that returns a boolean value.

    Predicates merely wrap their argument and remain unevaluated:

        >>> from sympy import Q, ask
        >>> type(Q.prime)
        <class 'sympy.assumptions.assume.Predicate'>
        >>> Q.prime.name
        'prime'
        >>> Q.prime(7)
        Q.prime(7)
        >>> _.func.name
        'prime'

    To obtain the truth value of an expression containing predicates, use
    the function ``ask``:

        >>> ask(Q.prime(7))
        True

    The tautological predicate ``Q.is_true`` can be used to wrap other objects:

        >>> from sympy.abc import x
        >>> Q.is_true(x > 1)
        Q.is_true(x > 1)

    """

    is_Atom = True

    def __new__(cls, name, handlers=None):
        obj = Boolean.__new__(cls)
        obj.name = name
        obj.handlers = handlers or []
        return obj

    def _hashable_content(self):
        return (self.name,)

class UnevaluatedOnFree(BooleanFunction):
    """
    Represents a Boolean function that remains unevaluated on free predicates

    This is intended to be a superclass of other classes, which define the
    behavior on singly applied predicates.

    A free predicate is a predicate that is not applied, or a combination
    thereof. For example, Q.zero or Or(Q.positive, Q.negative).

    A singly applied predicate is a free predicate applied everywhere to a
    single expression. For instance, Q.zero(x) and Or(Q.positive(x*y),
    Q.negative(x*y)) are singly applied, but Or(Q.positive(x), Q.negative(y))
    and Or(Q.positive, Q.negative(y)) are not.

    The boolean literals True and False are considered to be both free and
    singly applied.

    This class raises ValueError unless the input is a free predicate or a
    singly applied predicate.

    On a free predicate, this class remains unevaluated. On a singly applied
    predicate, the method apply() is called and returned, or the original
    expression returned if apply() returns None. When apply() is called,
    self.expr is set to the unique expression that the predicates are applied
    at. self.pred is set to the free form of the predicate.

    The typical usage is to create this class with free predicates and
    evaluate it using .rcall().

    """
    def __new__(cls, arg):
        # Mostly type checking here
        arg = _sympify(arg)
        predicates = arg.atoms(Predicate)
        applied_predicates = arg.atoms(AppliedPredicate)
        if predicates and applied_predicates:
            raise ValueError("arg must be either completely free or singly applied")
        if not applied_predicates:
            obj = BooleanFunction.__new__(cls, arg)
            obj.pred = arg
            obj.expr = None
            return obj
        predicate_args = {pred.args[0] for pred in applied_predicates}
        if len(predicate_args) > 1:
            raise ValueError("The AppliedPredicates in arg must be applied to a single expression.")
        obj = BooleanFunction.__new__(cls, arg)
        obj.expr = predicate_args.pop()
        obj.pred = arg.xreplace(Transform(lambda e: e.func, lambda e:
            isinstance(e, AppliedPredicate)))
        applied = obj.apply(obj.expr)
        if applied is None:
            return obj
        return applied

    def apply(self, expr=None):
        if expr is None:
            return
        pred = to_NNF(self.pred)
        return self._eval_apply(expr, pred)

    def _eval_apply(self, expr, pred):
        return None

def as_Boolean(e):

    which can be any instance of Boolean or bool.

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy import true, false, nan
    >>> from sympy.logic.boolalg import as_Boolean

    if e == False:

bug_report.Title: expr.atoms() (no-arg) returns Atom subclasses with args instead of true leaf nodes
bug_report.Description: Calling expr.atoms() with no arguments returns instances of Atom subclasses (isinstance(..., Atom)) even when those objects have non-empty .args. The method therefore does not return expression-tree leaves (objects whose .args == ()). This manifests in Basic.atoms and is reproduced at the Matrix level.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) sympy/core/basic.py::Basic.atoms encodes the incorrect assumption "Atom subclasses == leaf nodes" by using the literal default types = (Atom,) when no types are supplied. The method filters nodes with isinstance(expr, types), which includes Atom subclasses that expose .args. The correct selection for the no-types case is: iterate preorder_traversal(self) and add expr when not getattr(expr, 'args', ()). (Preserve variable names: types, Atom, preorder_traversal, expr.args.)

2) sympy/matrices/common.py::Matrix.atoms forces the same wrong default by setting types = (Atom,) when called without types and then calling self._eval_atoms(*types). This propagates the isinstance-based Atom filter to matrix elements even if Basic.atoms is changed. The correct relationship is: only convert and pass types when types is truthy; otherwise call self._eval_atoms() so element-level atoms() uses the leaf-based default.

3) The class-level flag is_Atom and the Atom subclass hierarchy are not a reliable definition of leaves: some classes set is_Atom = True yet have non-empty .args. Example evidence: sympy/assumptions/assume.py::AppliedPredicate sets is_Atom = True but represents applied predicates and carries arguments. Therefore isinstance(obj, Atom) does not imply obj.args == ().

4) The explicit-type branch must remain unchanged: calls of the form atoms(TypeA, TypeB, ...) must continue to collect instances by type. Only the no-argument (default) branch is incorrect and must select nodes with no .args.

5) The incorrect literal default to change is exactly the tuple assignment types = (Atom,) found in two locations: sympy/core/basic.py and sympy/matrices/common.py. A repo search returned only these two literal occurrences, limiting the scope of the change.

6) Exact selection logic that preserves current semantics for explicit types but changes the no-types behavior (as discovered in the investigation):
   - If types is truthy: convert entries with t if isinstance(t, type) else type(t); for expr in preorder_traversal(self): if isinstance(expr, types): result.add(expr).
   - Else (no types): for expr in preorder_traversal(self): if not getattr(expr, 'args', ()): result.add(expr).

7) Missing runtime verification: the investigation did not execute concrete REPL examples or test-suite/performance checks. These verification steps remain outstanding and are necessary to confirm behavioral and perf effects.
StepsToReproduce: Open a Python interpreter with the sympy package from the repository.
Construct or obtain an expression whose class is marked as an Atom subclass but has non-empty .args (for example, an AppliedPredicate or any class that sets is_Atom = True and exposes arguments).
Observe that the returned set includes the Atom-subclass instance(s) that have non-empty .args (i.e., non-leaf objects are present).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: expr.atoms() called with no arguments returns only leaf subexpressions — i.e., objects in the expression tree whose .args attribute is empty (expr.args == ()). The explicit-type form atoms(TypeA, ...) continues to return instances matching the given types.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: expr.atoms() returns Atom-subclass instances based on isinstance(..., Atom) even when those instances have non-empty .args, so non-leaf objects (Atom subclasses with arguments) appear in the result.

def _iszero(x):
    """Returns True if x is zero."""
    return x.is_zero


def _compare_sequence(a, b):
    """Compares the elements of a list/tuple `a`
    and a list/tuple `b`.  `_compare_sequence((1,2), [1, 2])`
    is True, whereas `(1,2) == [1, 2]` is False"""
    if type(a) is type(b):
        # if they are the same type, compare directly
        return a == b
    # there is no overhead for calling `tuple` on a
    # tuple
    return tuple(a) == tuple(b)

def _force_mutable(x):
    """Return a matrix as a Matrix, otherwise return x."""
    if getattr(x, 'is_Matrix', False):
        return x.as_mutable()
    elif isinstance(x, Basic):
        return x
    elif hasattr(x, '__array__'):
        a = x.__array__()
        if len(a.shape) == 0:
            return sympify(a)
        return Matrix(x)
    return x

    mats = self.args
    data = [[mats[i] if i == j else ZeroMatrix(mats[i].rows, mats[j].cols)
                    for j in range(len(mats))]

This is a single-line change: explicitly pass evaluate=False to ImmutableDenseMatrix, matching the pattern used elsewhere (e.g. BlockMatrix.__new__ uses ImmutableDenseMatrix(rows, evaluate=False)).

Why this fixes it
- When evaluate=False is passed, ImmutableDenseMatrix._handle_creation_inputs will not try to treat the inner Matrix objects as items to be concatenated/flattened into the outer matrix; instead it will construct a 1x1 ImmutableDenseMatrix whose sole entry is the Matrix M. Then BlockMatrix._entry will get self.blocks[0,0] = the Matrix M, and M[i,j] works fine, giving the intended explicit element. The erroneous scenario (self.blocks being M itself and self.blocks[0,0] returning S.One) disappears.

4a) "What assumption does my fix change?"
- The original code relied on the implicit behavior that ImmutableDenseMatrix(data) would create a 1x1 matrix-of-blocks when data = [[M]]; my fix removes that assumption by explicitly instructing ImmutableDenseMatrix not to evaluate/flatten nested matrices (evaluate=False), so the new assumption is that constructing an ImmutableDenseMatrix of block entries should be done with evaluate=False to preserve block objects as entries.

4b) "What hardcoded values encode this assumption?"
- The primary "hardcoded value" that encoded the old assumption is the implicit default evaluate=True in ImmutableDenseMatrix._new/_handle_creation_inputs. That default value causes nested Matrix entries to be expanded.
- In the component classes I inspected:
  - ImmutableDenseMatrix._new uses kwargs.get('copy', True) and delegates to _handle_creation_inputs by default; the choice evaluate=True is the default coded in matrices._handle_creation_inputs. If evaluate=False is not passed, flattening occurs.
  - There were no other numeric hardcoded values that depend on the assumption. ZeroMatrix uses S.One and S.Zero but those are independent and remain correct.

bug_report.Title: Converting a single-block BlockDiagMatrix to Matrix raises TypeError ('One' object is not subscriptable)
bug_report.Description: When a BlockDiagMatrix is constructed with exactly one Matrix element and then converted to a concrete Matrix (Matrix(BlockDiagMatrix(M))), a TypeError is raised because the BlockDiagMatrix implementation constructs the block container in a way that allows the nested Matrix to be expanded/concatenated into a numeric matrix instead of preserved as a 1×1 matrix-of-blocks.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) sympy/matrices/expressions/blockmatrix.py:BlockDiagMatrix.blocks — incorrect construction of the blocks container: the code builds a nested Python list 'data' containing the diagonal block(s) (for a single block, data == [[M]]) and then calls ImmutableDenseMatrix(data) (no evaluate flag). Exact code: 'data = [[mats[i] if i == j else ZeroMatrix(...) for j in range(len(mats))] for i in range(len(mats))]' and 'return ImmutableDenseMatrix(data)'. The code thereby assumes that ImmutableDenseMatrix(data) will preserve the inner Matrix M as a single element of a 1×1 matrix-of-blocks; that assumption is false when the default evaluation behavior is used.

2) sympy/matrices/matrices.py:Matrix._handle_creation_inputs and sympy/matrices/immutable.py:ImmutableDenseMatrix._new — default evaluation behavior flattens nested Matrix objects: Matrix._handle_creation_inputs uses 'evaluate = kwargs.get("evaluate", True)' and contains explicit logic that, when evaluate is True, treats MatrixBase entries as submatrices to be concatenated into the outer matrix (e.g. 'flat_list = [_ for i in dat for r in i.tolist() for _ in r]' and the recursive transpose/reshape path for list-of-lists of matrices). ImmutableDenseMatrix._new delegates to _handle_creation_inputs, so calling ImmutableDenseMatrix(data) with the default evaluate=True will expand [[M]] into M's numeric entries rather than preserving [[M]] as a 1×1 matrix-of-blocks.

3) sympy/matrices/expressions/blockmatrix.py:BlockMatrix._entry — usage assumption that is violated by the flattening: BlockMatrix._entry locates the block indices and then indexes into the block with 'return self.blocks[row_block, col_block][i, j]'. This code assumes that self.blocks[row_block, col_block] is a Matrix-like object (supports [i, j]). If BlockDiagMatrix.blocks allowed ImmutableDenseMatrix to expand the inner M, then self.blocks[0,0] becomes a scalar (e.g. S.One) or other non-matrix element, so the subsequent '[i, j]' subscript raises TypeError: 'One' object is not subscriptable, which matches the observed exception.

4) sympy/matrices/expressions/blockmatrix.py:BlockMatrix.__new (correct pattern evidence) — elsewhere where a matrix-of-blocks is intended, the code constructs the ImmutableDenseMatrix with evaluate=False: 'mat = ImmutableDenseMatrix(rows, evaluate=False)'. This demonstrates the intended relationship: ImmutableDenseMatrix(..., evaluate=False) preserves nested Matrix objects as elements of the matrix rather than concatenating their entries. The defect is that BlockDiagMatrix.blocks does not use evaluate=False while BlockMatrix.__new does.

Diagnostic relationship/constant: The default evaluate behavior for ImmutableDenseMatrix (evaluate=True) concatenates nested Matrix objects into the outer matrix's entries; to preserve nested Matrix objects as elements of a matrix-of-blocks, the creation must be performed with evaluate=False (i.e., the value of the 'evaluate' keyword determines whether nested matrices are flattened or preserved).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Converting a BlockDiagMatrix containing a single Matrix block to an explicit Matrix should produce the same Matrix M (Matrix(BlockDiagMatrix(M)) == M) without raising exceptions.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Matrix(BlockDiagMatrix(M)) raises TypeError: 'One' object is not subscriptable. The conversion path attempts to subscript a scalar because the block container was flattened instead of preserving the inner Matrix as a block.
